title: How Thailand’s Limestone Islands Formed
subtitle: From an ancient seabed to the dramatic towers of Phang Nga Bay
description: Discover how ancient sea sediments became limestone, how rainwater carved tall rock towers, and why those towers now rise from the sea. Practise useful English with Armenian vocabulary support, reading questions, and speaking prompts.
excerpt: Ancient seabed. Rising land. Rain-carved towers. A returning sea. Follow the extraordinary story of Thailand’s limestone islands while building your English.
originalMarkdown:
If you mean **the tall, steep rocky hills sticking out of the sea around Phuket and Phang Nga Bay**, those are **limestone karst islands**—including the huge rock beside Koh Panyee.

Their story is fascinating: **the rock formed beneath an ancient sea, was lifted onto land, was slowly carved into towers, and then became surrounded by seawater again.** [Department of Mineral Resources: The Invaluable Natural Heritage — Ao Phangnga](https://www.dmr.go.th/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/article_20170622105315-1.pdf)

## 1. First, the rock formed underwater 🐚

Around **250–300 million years ago**, the limestone that makes up these formations began developing in an ancient sea.

Carbonate mud and the remains of marine organisms accumulated on the seabed. Over a very long time, those sediments became solid **limestone**. Geologists can still find fossils of ancient sea creatures, including corals, in the limestone around Phang Nga Bay. [Department of Mineral Resources: The Invaluable Natural Heritage — Ao Phangnga](https://www.dmr.go.th/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/article_20170622105315-1.pdf) · [Department of Mineral Resources: Geology of Phang-nga Province](https://www.dmr.go.th/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/03-guidebook_Phung-Nga.pdf)

So the material making up those enormous cliffs has its origins in an ancient marine environment.

## 2. Movements of the Earth lifted it above the sea

As the Earth’s tectonic plates moved, they pushed and deformed the rock, raising it above sea level.

The limestone became part of a land landscape. Further movements created **faults and cracks** through it. These cracks were important because they gave water pathways into the rock. [Department of Mineral Resources: The Invaluable Natural Heritage — Ao Phangnga](https://www.dmr.go.th/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/article_20170622105315-1.pdf)

## 3. Rainwater slowly carved the hills 🌧️

This is the part that explains their unusual shapes.

**Limestone gradually dissolves in slightly acidic water.** Rainwater picks up carbon dioxide from the air and especially from soil, forming a weak acid. As this water enters cracks, it slowly dissolves and carries away the limestone.

Over immense periods of time:

- Small cracks widen into larger openings.
- Underground passages and caves develop.
- Depressions deepen and the surrounding land wears away.
- Remaining masses of limestone stand above the lowered ground as steep hills and towers.

That kind of landscape is called **karst**. Thailand’s wet tropical climate and abundant vegetation help these processes operate. [Marcus Gillespie: Tower Karst of Peninsular Thailand](https://www.siue.edu/GEOGRAPHY/ONLINE/Gillespie.htm)

**Imagine a large block of stone being gradually eaten away along its cracks, leaving several tall pieces standing.** That gives you a useful picture of how a connected limestone landscape can become a collection of separate towers.

## 4. Rising seawater surrounded the towers 🌊

After the last ice age, melting ice raised sea levels. In Phang Nga Bay, seawater flooded lower parts of the landscape, particularly during the period approximately **10,000–6,000 years ago**.

The surviving limestone hills became islands, with their lower portions underwater. That is why they appear to rise so abruptly from the sea today. [Department of Mineral Resources: The Invaluable Natural Heritage — Ao Phangnga](https://www.dmr.go.th/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/article_20170622105315-1.pdf)

The **rock is hundreds of millions of years old**; its present appearance as an island developed much later.

## Why are some narrower at the bottom?

If you look near the waterline, you may notice grooves, overhangs, or bases that look as though something has taken a bite out of them.

The tidal zone continues to wear away through physical erosion and the activity of organisms that scrape or bore into the limestone. Measurements taken over ten years in Phang Nga Bay show that this erosion is still happening. [Moses and colleagues: Ten years of limestone erosion measurements in Phang Nga Bay](https://research.edgehill.ac.uk/en/publications/towards-an-improved-understanding-of-erosion-rates-and-tidal-notc-2/)

The famous **Ko Tapu pillar near James Bond Island** is a striking example of continued coastal reshaping: erosion separated it from the neighbouring rock, leaving the narrow, isolated sea stack you see today. [Department of Mineral Resources: The Invaluable Natural Heritage — Ao Phangnga](https://www.dmr.go.th/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/article_20170622105315-1.pdf)

vocabulary.definition: A rock made mainly of calcium carbonate, often formed from material deposited in ancient seas.
vocabulary.example: Much of the rock in Phang Nga Bay is limestone.

vocabulary.definition: A landscape with caves, hollows, or towers formed as water dissolves rock such as limestone.
vocabulary.armenian: կարստ՝ լուծվող ապարների քայքայումից առաջացած ռելիեֆ
vocabulary.example: The steep towers are part of a karst landscape.

vocabulary.definition: Related to the sea or the things that live in it.
vocabulary.example: Corals and many other marine organisms leave hard remains behind.

vocabulary.definition: Small pieces of material that settle at the bottom of water or collect on land.
vocabulary.example: Layers of sediment accumulated on the ancient seabed.

vocabulary.definition: The ground at the bottom of the sea.
vocabulary.example: Mud and the remains of sea creatures collected on the seabed.

vocabulary.definition: The preserved remains or trace of a plant or animal from the distant past.
vocabulary.armenian: բրածո՝ հնագույն օրգանիզմի պահպանված մնացորդ կամ հետք
vocabulary.example: A coral fossil can provide evidence of an ancient sea.

vocabulary.definition: One of the large, slowly moving pieces of the Earth’s outer shell.
vocabulary.example: A moving tectonic plate can push and deform rock.

vocabulary.definition: A break in the Earth’s rock along which the rock has moved.
vocabulary.example: Movement along a fault can change the position of rock layers.

vocabulary.definition: A narrow break or opening in a surface.
vocabulary.example: Rainwater entered the limestone through a crack.

vocabulary.definition: To become mixed into a liquid, or to make a substance do this.
vocabulary.example: Slightly acidic water can dissolve limestone.

vocabulary.definition: Containing acid or having the properties of an acid.
vocabulary.example: Water becomes slightly acidic when carbon dioxide dissolves in it.

vocabulary.definition: A gas found in air and soil that can form a weak acid when it dissolves in water.
vocabulary.example: Rainwater picks up carbon dioxide as it passes through the soil.

vocabulary.definition: The plants growing in a particular place.
vocabulary.example: The island’s upper slopes are covered in vegetation.

vocabulary.definition: A route or narrow space through which people, water, or other things can pass.
vocabulary.example: Water gradually enlarged an underground passage.

vocabulary.definition: An area of land that is lower than the ground around it.
vocabulary.example: A depression became deeper as the limestone dissolved.

vocabulary.definition: The gradual wearing away and removal of rock or soil.
vocabulary.armenian: էրոզիա՝ ապարների կամ հողի քայքայում և հեռացում
vocabulary.example: Coastal erosion continues to change the shape of the rock.

vocabulary.definition: A high, steep face of rock.
vocabulary.example: The boat passed beside a tall limestone cliff.

vocabulary.definition: The height of the sea’s surface, used as a reference for measuring land height.
vocabulary.example: Sea level rose as ice melted after the last ice age.

vocabulary.definition: To cover land that is usually dry with water.
vocabulary.example: Rising seawater began to flood the lower ground.

vocabulary.definition: The line where the surface of water meets land, rock, or an object.
vocabulary.armenian: ջրագիծ՝ ջրի մակերևույթի և առարկայի հատման գիծ
vocabulary.example: Look near the waterline to see the grooves in the rock.

vocabulary.definition: A part of something that sticks out beyond the part below it.
vocabulary.example: The cliff has an overhang above the water.

vocabulary.definition: Related to the regular rise and fall of the sea.
vocabulary.example: The tidal zone is affected by the sea’s changing level.

vocabulary.definition: To make a hole in something by digging or drilling into it.
vocabulary.example: Some small organisms bore into limestone.

vocabulary.definition: An isolated, steep pillar of rock standing in the sea near a coast.
vocabulary.example: Ko Tapu is a narrow sea stack in Phang Nga Bay.

quiz.question: What kind of rock mainly forms the tall islands described in the article?
options: Granite
Limestone
Volcanic lava
Sand
quiz.explanation: The formations are limestone karst islands. Their rock formed from carbonate material deposited in an ancient sea.

quiz.question: Where did the material that became the limestone originally accumulate?
options: On the seabed of an ancient sea
Inside a volcano
On a glacier
In a modern city
quiz.explanation: Carbonate mud and the remains of marine organisms accumulated on the seabed before becoming solid limestone.

quiz.question: Why were faults and cracks important in shaping the limestone?
options: They stopped all water from entering.
They turned the rock into ice.
They gave water pathways into the rock.
They made the rock float.
quiz.explanation: Water could enter faults and cracks, gradually dissolve limestone, and enlarge the openings.

quiz.question: How does rainwater become slightly acidic in the process described?
options: It picks up salt from passing boats.
It freezes inside the rock.
It becomes warmer in sunlight.
It picks up carbon dioxide from the air and soil.
quiz.explanation: Carbon dioxide dissolves in rainwater and forms a weak acid, which helps the water dissolve limestone.

quiz.question: Which sequence best matches the article?
options: Sea rises → rock forms → rain falls → land rises
Rock forms underwater → land rises → water carves towers → sea floods the lower ground
Towers float → sea freezes → caves disappear → rock forms
Waves make sand → sand becomes ice → ice becomes towers → sea falls
quiz.explanation: The article describes ancient marine limestone, uplift onto land, long-term karst development, and later flooding of the lower landscape.

quiz.question: What does the article say about the age of the rock and its present island shape?
options: Both appeared only ten years ago.
The island shape is older than the rock.
The rock is hundreds of millions of years old; its present island appearance developed later.
They both formed during the last ice age.
quiz.explanation: The limestone is approximately 250–300 million years old. The surrounding landscape was flooded much later, particularly about 10,000–6,000 years ago.

quiz.question: Why can some rock formations become narrower near the waterline?
options: Physical erosion and organisms continue to wear away the rock.
The upper parts are filled with air.
Plants pull the bottom upward.
The sea permanently protects the base from erosion.
quiz.explanation: Erosion and organisms that scrape or bore into limestone continue to modify the tidal zone.

quiz.question: What does “karst” describe in this article?
options: A type of boat used in Thailand
A layer of frozen seawater
A particular species of coral
A landscape shaped by the dissolution of rock such as limestone
quiz.explanation: Karst forms as water dissolves soluble rock, producing features such as caves, depressions, steep hills, and towers.

cloze.sentence: Mud and the remains of sea creatures collected on the ____ at the bottom of the sea.
cloze.hint: A noun meaning the ground beneath the sea.

cloze.sentence: Over a very long time, those sediments became solid ____.
cloze.hint: The main type of rock in the islands described.
A verb meaning to make a substance become mixed into a liquid.

cloze.sentence: Water entered the rock through faults and ____.
cloze.hint: Narrow breaks in a surface; use the plural form.

cloze.sentence: As sea levels rose, seawater began to ____ the lower ground.
cloze.hint: A verb meaning to cover land with water.

cloze.sentence: The gradual wearing away and removal of rock is called ____.

speaking.prompt: Describe the limestone islands to a friend who has never seen them. Speak for 30–45 seconds.
speaking.tip: Use three or more of these words: steep, cliff, limestone, vegetation, sea.

speaking.prompt: Explain the four main stages of the islands’ formation in your own words.
speaking.tip: Organize your answer with first, then, over time, and finally. Keep the order: seabed, uplift, karst, rising sea.

speaking.prompt: Explain why the rock can be hundreds of millions of years old while its present island appearance is much younger.
speaking.tip: Begin with “The rock formed…” and then contrast it with “The hills became islands when…”

speaking.prompt: A visitor asks, “Why is the bottom of that rock so narrow?” Give a short, clear answer.
speaking.tip: Mention the waterline, erosion, and organisms. Try using because to explain a cause.

speaking.prompt: Imagine you are a guide in Phang Nga Bay. Explain how rainwater can change solid rock, then ask your visitor one question.
speaking.tip: Use crack, acidic, and dissolve. A possible question opening is “Can you imagine how long…?”

grammar.title: Past simple passive: was formed, were flooded
grammar.explanation: Use was or were + the past participle when the thing affected is the focus. Scientific explanations often use the passive to describe what happened to rock, land, or water. Use was with a singular subject and were with a plural subject.
examples: The limestone was lifted above sea level.
The lower ground was flooded by seawater.
The towers were surrounded by water.
grammar.exercise: Complete the sentence with the past simple passive: “The rock ____ (lift) above sea level millions of years ago.”

grammar.title: Connect events with after and because
grammar.explanation: Use after to show the order of events. Use because to give a reason. When an after-clause comes first, place a comma before the main clause. These connectors help you explain a process clearly.
examples: After the ice melted, sea levels rose.
After seawater flooded the lower ground, the hills became islands.
The cracks were important because they allowed water into the rock.
grammar.exercise: Choose after or because: “The cracks widened ____ water slowly dissolved the limestone.”
